claim: Multi-ciliated epithelial cells (MCCs) are critical for proper development and homeostasis of the airway, brain and reproductive tracts.
source: Starting from genomic analysis of the cilia-associated transcription factor Rfx2, we used bioinformatics and in vivo cell biological approaches to gain insights into the molecular basis of cilia assembly and function. Moreover, we discovered a previously un-recognized role for an Rfx factor in cell movement, finding that Rfx2 cell-autonomously controls apical surface expansion in nascent MCCs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background context for the study.

claim: Rfx2 cell-autonomously controls apical surface expansion in nascent MCCs.
source: Moreover, we discovered a previously un-recognized role for an Rfx factor in cell movement, finding that Rfx2 cell-autonomously controls apical surface expansion in nascent MCCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including live imaging and transplantation experiments shown in Figures 5-6.

claim: Rfx2 coordinates multiple, distinct gene expression programs in MCCs, regulating genes that control cell movement, ciliogenesis, and cilia function.
source: Thus, Rfx2 coordinates multiple, distinct gene expression programs in MCCs, regulating genes that control cell movement, ciliogenesis, and cilia function.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the combined RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Hundreds of proteins are required for cilia assembly and function.
source: Recent studies of cilia and ciliated epithelial cells highlight the current disconnect between genomics and cell biology: it is clear that hundreds of proteins are required for cilia assembly and function (Gherman et al., 2006; Inglis et al., 2006), and moreover, assembly of new cilia/flagella clearly requires new transcription (Thomas et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Gherman et al., 2006; Inglis et al., 2006).

claim: Assembly of new cilia/flagella requires new transcription.
source: Recent studies of cilia and ciliated epithelial cells highlight the current disconnect between genomics and cell biology: it is clear that hundreds of proteins are required for cilia assembly and function (Gherman et al., 2006; Inglis et al., 2006), and moreover, assembly of new cilia/flagella clearly requires new transcription (Thomas et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Thomas et al., 2010.

claim: In C. elegans, the sole RFX family transcription factor daf-19 is the central regulator of ciliogenesis.
source: In C. elegans, the sole RFX family transcription factor daf-19 is the central regulator of ciliogenesis, and dozens of target genes are known to effect its action (Efimenko et al., 2005; Phirke et al., 2011; Burghoorn et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Efimenko et al., 2005; Phirke et al., 2011; Burghoorn et al., 2012).

claim: Multiple RFX family members are essential for ciliogenesis in vertebrates.
source: By contrast, multiple RFX family members are essential for ciliogenesis in vertebrates, but as yet, there has been no comprehensive genome-wide survey of Rfx-dependent gene expression as it relates to ciliogenesis (Bonnafe et al., 2004; Ashique et al., 2009; El Zein et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Bonnafe et al., 2004; Ashique et al., 2009; El Zein et al., 2009).

claim: Multi-ciliated epithelial cells project dozens or hundreds of motile cilia from their apical surfaces.
source: These cells project dozens or hundreds of motile cilia from their apical surfaces, and the polarized beating of these cilia generates fluid flow that is essential for development and homeostasis in many organ systems (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a descriptive claim about MCC structure, supported by reference to Figure 1 which illustrates this feature.

claim: MCCs are central to the normal homeostasis of airway, brain and reproductive tracts.
source: Such cells are central to the normal homeostasis of airway, brain and reproductive tracts (Worthington and Cathcart, 1963; Yeung et al., 1991; Lyons et al., 2006; Fahy and Dickey, 2010), and defective functioning of these cells is associated with pathologies ranging from chronic infection to hydrocephalus (Afzelius, 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies (Worthington and Cathcart, 1963; Yeung et al., 1991; Lyons et al., 2006; Fahy and Dickey, 2010).

claim: Defective functioning of MCCs is associated with pathologies ranging from chronic infection to hydrocephalus.
source: Such cells are central to the normal homeostasis of airway, brain and reproductive tracts (Worthington and Cathcart, 1963; Yeung et al., 1991; Lyons et al., 2006; Fahy and Dickey, 2010), and defective functioning of these cells is associated with pathologies ranging from chronic infection to hydrocephalus (Afzelius, 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Afzelius, 1976.

claim: Rfx2 is essential for the normal development of cilia in MCCs.
source: We therefore exploited the Xenopus system to perform parallel RNA transcript sequencing (RNA-seq) and chromatin immunoprecipitation deep sequencing (ChIP-seq) for Rfx2, which we showed previously to be essential for the normal development of cilia in MCCs (Chung et al., 2012) (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Chung et al., 2012).

claim: 2750 genes were differentially expressed following Rfx2 knockdown (>twofold; FDR<0.05).
source: From this list of 11,644 genes, we identified 2750 genes that were differentially expressed following Rfx2 knockdown (>twofold; FDR<0.05) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by RNA-seq experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 3465 genes were significantly bound by Rfx2.
source: We identified 3465 genes that were significantly bound by Rfx2 and, importantly, this set of genes overlapped significantly with the set of genes differentially expressed in Rfx2 morphants (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 3) (p≤10−6, hypergeometric test).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by ChIP-seq experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The set of genes bound by Rfx2 overlapped significantly with the set of genes differentially expressed in Rfx2 morphants (p≤10−6, hypergeometric test).
source: We identified 3465 genes that were significantly bound by Rfx2 and, importantly, this set of genes overlapped significantly with the set of genes differentially expressed in Rfx2 morphants (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 3) (p≤10−6, hypergeometric test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data.

claim: 911 genes are directly regulated downstream target genes of Rfx2.
source: The intersection of these two experiments defined 911 genes (Figure 2—source data 1), corresponding to the directly regulated downstream target genes of Rfx2.
evidence: This claim is supported by the intersection of RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data.

claim: 100% of tested directly bound, differentially expressed genes were confirmed as Rfx2-dependent genes by in situ hybridization and RT-PCR analysis.
source: We tested a subset of these directly bound, differentially expressed genes by in situ hybridization and RT-PCR analysis; 100% were confirmed as Rfx2-dependent genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by validation experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Components of essentially all known ciliary machinery are under the control of Rfx2 in MCCs.
source: Moreover, direct examination of the 911 Rfx2 target genes revealed that components of essentially all known ciliary machinery are under the control of Rfx2 in MCCs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the Rfx2 target gene list presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Rfx2 directly controls expression of IFT-B complex components ift172 and ift88.
source: IFT involves two separable complexes, IFT-A and IFT-B (Pedersen and Rosenbaum, 2008), and we identified the IFT–B complex components ift172 and ift88 as direct Rfx2 targets, consistent with data from flies, worms, and mice (Thomas et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data, and is consistent with previous studies (Thomas et al., 2010).

claim: Rfx2 directly controls expression of genes encoding axonemal dynein subunits, components of the transition zone, and a component of the BBSome.
source: Additionally, we found that Rfx2 directly controls expression of genes encoding axonemal dynein subunits, components of the transition zone, and a component of the BBSome, and many of these genes are mutated in human ciliopathies (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 1A) (Sharma et al., 2008; Reiter et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data presented in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: Many Rfx2 target genes are mutated in human ciliopathies.
source: Additionally, we found that Rfx2 directly controls expression of genes encoding axonemal dynein subunits, components of the transition zone, and a component of the BBSome, and many of these genes are mutated in human ciliopathies (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 1A) (Sharma et al., 2008; Reiter et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Sharma et al., 2008; Reiter et al., 2012) and the data in this manuscript.

claim: Rfx2 controlled expression of tubulins, enzymes involved in tubulin post-translational modification, and microtubule binding proteins.
source: For example, Rfx2 controlled expression of tubulins, enzymes involved in tubulin post-translational modification, and microtubule binding proteins, such as map7 and spef1/clamp, which localize to the proximal and distal axonemes, respectively (Brooks and Wallingford, 2012) (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data presented in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: Rfx2 controls the expression of the planar cell polarity (PCP) effector gene fritz/wdpcp.
source: Rfx2 also controlled the expression of the planar cell polarity (PCP) effector gene fritz/wdpcp, which encodes a protein governing assembly of the septin diffusion barrier at the base of cilia (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data, and is consistent with previous studies (Kim et al., 2010).

claim: Rfx2 controls many centriolar genes required for ciliogenesis, including cep164.
source: Rfx2 also controls many centriolar genes required for ciliogenesis, including cep164 (Graser et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data, and is consistent with previous studies (Graser et al., 2007).

claim: wdpcp and cep164 are both implicated in human ciliopathies.
source: Notably, wdpcp and cep164 are both implicated in human ciliopathies (Kim et al., 2010; Chaki et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Kim et al., 2010; Chaki et al., 2012).

claim: Ttc29 is a candidate for functional interaction with the IFT machinery based on HumanNet analysis.
source: Using 'guilt-by-association' in this network, we identified ttc29 as a candidate for functional interaction with the IFT machinery (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is based on bioinformatic analysis using the HumanNet gene network.

claim: Ttc29-GFP localized to ciliary axonemes.
source: We tested this prediction and found not only that Ttc29-GFP localized to ciliary axonemes, but also that knockdown elicited substantial defects in ciliogenesis (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Ttc29 knockdown elicited substantial defects in ciliogenesis.
source: We tested this prediction and found not only that Ttc29-GFP localized to ciliary axonemes, but also that knockdown elicited substantial defects in ciliogenesis (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Partial knockdown of Ttc29 resulted in a significant decrease in the mean rate of anterograde IFT.
source: Strikingly, partial knockdown of Ttc29 resulted in a significant decrease in the mean rate of anterograde IFT (Figure 3E–G; Video 1), consistent with the bioinformatic linkage of ttc29 to components of the anterograde IFT-B complex (ift88 and ttc30a; Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Retrograde IFT movement was not significantly affected by Ttc29 knockdown.
source: Retrograde IFT movement was not significantly affected by Ttc29 knockdown (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The most strongly enriched biological process GO term among Rfx2 target genes was 'ciliary or flagellar motility'.
source: Of these, the most strongly enriched biological process GO term was 'ciliary or flagellar motility' (Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis of the Rfx2 target genes.

claim: Rfx2 controls a wide range of genes with known roles in cilia beating, including genes implicated in planar polarization of cilia (frizzled, prickle).
source: A direct exploration of the Rfx2 targets identified a wide range of genes with known roles in cilia beating, including genes implicated in planar polarization of cilia (frizzled, prickle) (Mitchell et al., 2009; Vladar et al., 2012), tubulin polyglutamylases governing inner arm dynein activity (ttll7, ttll9, ttll13), dynein regulatory complex components, radial spoke components, and a variety of poorly-understood cilia beating genes, such as ropn1l, mns1, pacrg, and hydin (Lechtreck et al., 2008; Wilson et al., 2010; Fiedler et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012) (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data presented in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1B, along with citations to previous studies.

claim: Unbiased clustering predicted that three known ciliary beating genes (dnai1, ropn1l, mns1) should be functionally linked to ribc2.
source: Unbiased clustering predicted that three known ciliary beating genes (dnai1, ropn1l, mns1) (Horvath et al., 2005; Fiedler et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012) should be functionally linked to ribc2, which encodes an uncharacterized vertebrate protein with similarity to Chlamydomonas protofilament ribbon proteins (Linck and Norrander, 2003) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is based on bioinformatic analysis using the HumanNet gene network.

claim: Ribc2 localized to axonemes.
source: Using a GFP-fusion, we found that Ribc2 localized to axonemes, though knockdown did not substantially affect cilia length (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Ribc2 knockdown did not substantially affect cilia length.
source: Using a GFP-fusion, we found that Ribc2 localized to axonemes, though knockdown did not substantially affect cilia length (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: High-speed in vivo imaging revealed a specific defect in ciliary beating following disruption of Ribc2 function.
source: Rather, high-speed in vivo imaging of axonemes and analysis of fluid flow revealed a specific defect in ciliary beating following disruption of Ribc2 function (Figure 4E–H; Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4E-H and Videos 3 and 4.

claim: Loss of Ribc2 did not affect the integrity of outer doublet or central pair microtubules, but did disrupt their organization within the axoneme and the apparent number of dynein arms.
source: Transmission electron microscopy revealed that loss of Ribc2 did not affect the integrity of outer doublet or central pair microtubules, but did disrupt their organization within the axoneme and the apparent number of dynein arms (Figure 4I,J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by TEM data shown in Figure 4I-J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ribc2 is essential for the normal axonemal localization of Tekt2.
source: Little is known about protofilament ribbon proteins in any system (Linck and Norrander, 2003), but guided by connections in HumanNet (Figure 4A), we found that Ribc2 is essential for the normal axonemal localization of another protofilament ribbon protein, Tekt2 (Figure 4K–M).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4K-M.

claim: Nme5 has a cilia beating function.
source: Moreover, our approach also led us to assign a cilia beating function to the previously uncharacterized kinase Nme5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and to find that proper localization of this kinase within axonemes is Ribc2-dependent (Figure 4N).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Proper localization of Nme5 within axonemes is Ribc2-dependent.
source: Moreover, our approach also led us to assign a cilia beating function to the previously uncharacterized kinase Nme5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and to find that proper localization of this kinase within axonemes is Ribc2-dependent (Figure 4N).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4N.

claim: Ribc2 knockdown did not affect the normal axonemal localization of Pacrg protein.
source: By contrast, pacrg is another direct target of Rfx2 that is required for cilia motility (Wilson et al., 2010) but is not linked to ribc2 in HumanNet, and Ribc2 knockdown did not affect the normal axonemal localization of Pacrg protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Only ∼20% of the 911 Rfx2 target genes are present in known cilia proteomes.
source: Interestingly however, of the 911 Rfx2 target genes, only ∼20% are present in known cilia proteomes (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the Rfx2 target gene list with known cilia proteomes, as shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Many of the Rfx2 target genes are NOT involved in ciliogenesis or cilia function.
source: This finding suggests that many of the Rfx2 target genes are NOT involved in ciliogenesis or cilia function, a notion that is intriguing in light of recent reports of cilia-independent roles for 'ciliary' RFX genes (e.g., Senti and Swoboda, 2008; Ait-Lounis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 5A and citations to previous studies.

claim: Analysis of GO terms associated with Rfx2 target genes suggested a potential role for Rfx2 in cell movement and cell morphogenesis.
source: Analysis of GO terms associated with Rfx2 target genes suggested a potential role for Rfx2 in cell movement and cell morphogenesis (Figure 5A, Figure 2—source data 2), which is of interest because both Xenopus MCCs and their counterparts in mammalian airways arise from a population of p63-expressing basal precursor cells (Figure 1, red cell at right) (Evans and Moller, 1991; Drysdale and Elinson, 1992; Lu et al., 2001; Rock et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on Gene Ontology analysis of the Rfx2 target genes.

claim: Strong knockdowns of Rfx2 consistently resulted in MCCs being positioned well below the apical surface of the epithelium.
source: Consistent with a role for Rfx2 in the apical movement of MCCs, we found that strong knockdowns consistently resulted in MCCs being positioned well below the apical surface of the epithelium (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: The effect of Rfx2 on MCC positioning was not secondary to a ciliogenesis defect.
source: This effect was not secondary to a ciliogenesis defect, as milder knockdowns with lower doses of MO did not inhibit MCC emergence but did suppress ciliogenesis (Chung et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to previous work (Chung et al., 2012) and experimental design considerations.

claim: MCCs first engaged in a probing of neighboring cell–cell boundaries; subsequently, this behavior ceased and MCCs smoothly expanded their apical surfaces.
source: We identified two broad categories of MCC behavior associated with apical insertion. MCCs first engaged in a probing of neighboring cell–cell boundaries; subsequently, this behavior ceased and MCCs smoothly expanded their apical surfaces (Figure 5D; Videos 5 and 6).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5D and Videos 5 and 6.

claim: Time-lapse imaging in Rfx2 morphants revealed that the initial probing behavior was qualitatively normal, while the latter phase of apical surface expansion failed completely.
source: Time-lapse imaging in Rfx2 morphants revealed that the initial probing behavior was qualitatively normal, while the latter phase of apical surface expansion failed completely (Figure 5E; Video 7).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5E and Video 7.

claim: Rfx2 cell-autonomously controls the process of MCC apical surface expansion.
source: Knockdown of Rfx2 in the MCCs led to a robust failure of MCC apical surface expansion while knockdown in overlying superficial cells had no effect (Figure 6). Thus our data suggest that Rfx2 cell-autonomously controls the process of MCC apical surface expansion.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by transplantation experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Rfx2 directly regulates the extracellular matrix component dystroglycan (dag1).
source: Consistent with the observed insertion defects, we found that Rfx2 directly regulates the extracellular matrix component dystroglycan (dag1), which is a known regulator of MCC insertion (Sirour et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data, and is consistent with previous studies (Sirour et al., 2011).

claim: Rfx2 directly controlled transcription of both the slit2 ligand and the intracellular effector srgap2.
source: Interestingly, Dag1 is known to functionally interact with the Slit/Robo signaling system to control cellular morphogenesis in diverse settings (Medioni et al., 2008; Wright et al., 2012), so it was notable that Rfx2 directly controlled transcription of both the slit2 ligand and the intracellular effector srgap2 (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data presented in Supplementary file 1C.

claim: Slit2 knockdown disrupted insertion of nascent MCCs into the mucociliary epithelium.
source: Accordingly, we found that Slit2 knockdown disrupted insertion of nascent MCCs into the mucociliary epithelium and analysis of mosaic embryos revealed that Slit2 acts cell-autonomously in MCC insertion, as was the case for Rfx2 (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Slit2 acts cell-autonomously in MCC insertion.
source: Accordingly, we found that Slit2 knockdown disrupted insertion of nascent MCCs into the mucociliary epithelium and analysis of mosaic embryos revealed that Slit2 acts cell-autonomously in MCC insertion, as was the case for Rfx2 (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by mosaic analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Rfx2 and FoxJ1 are downstream of Mcidas.
source: Mcidas has been implicated in the earliest stages of MCC specification (Stubbs et al., 2012), and accordingly, both Rfx2 and FoxJ1 are downstream of Mcidas, while Mcidas is not present in the target gene sets of the other two factors.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of gene expression data from this study with previous studies (Stubbs et al., 2012).

claim: Many ciliary machines require the combined action of all or a subset of Rfx2, FoxJ1, and Mcidas.
source: Interestingly, our comparison suggests that many ciliary machines require the combined action of all or a subset of these three factors. For example, ift80 is downstream of all three factors, while Ift46 and ift57 are present only in the FoxJ1 gene set and ift140, ift172, ift81, and ift88 are targets only of Rfx2.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of gene expression data from this study with previous studies.

claim: Rfx2 plays essential roles in ciliogenesis that are independent of FoxJ1 or Mcidas.
source: Nonetheless, our data also suggest that Rfx2 also plays essential roles in ciliogenesis that are independent of FoxJ1 or Mcidas, as many IFT genes and several ciliopathy-associated genes (cep164, rpgripl1 and cc2d2a) are under the sole control of Rfx2 (Figure 8, left).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of gene expression data from this study with previous studies, as shown in Figure 8.

claim: The MCC insertion genes dag1 and slit2 were present only in the Rfx2 target gene list and were not identified as downstream targets of FoxJ1 or Mcidas.
source: Moreover, we have discovered a role here for Rfx2 in apical surface assembly of nascent MCCs, and Foxj1 has no known role in this process. Accordingly, the MCC insertion genes dag1 and slit2 were present only in the Rfx2 target gene list and were not identified as downstream targets of FoxJ1 or Mcidas.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of gene expression data from this study with previous studies.

claim: Rab11 is required for MCC insertion but was not present among Rfx2 targets.
source: Interestingly however, Rab11 is also required for MCC insertion (Kim et al., 2012), but was not present among our Rfx2 targets.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with previous studies (Kim et al., 2012) and the Rfx2 target gene list.

claim: Dag1 and Slit/Robo signaling collaborate during axon growth cone guidance.
source: These results are of particular interest both because Dag1 and Slit/Robo signaling also collaborate during axon growth cone guidance (Andrews et al., 2006; Wright et al., 2012) and because Rfx3 mutant mice display axon guidance defects (Benadiba et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Andrews et al., 2006; Wright et al., 2012).

claim: Rfx3 mutant mice display axon guidance defects.
source: These results are of particular interest both because Dag1 and Slit/Robo signaling also collaborate during axon growth cone guidance (Andrews et al., 2006; Wright et al., 2012) and because Rfx3 mutant mice display axon guidance defects (Benadiba et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Benadiba et al., 2012).

claim: Mammalian MCCs arise from basally-positioned precursor cells.
source: Finally, both the genomic studies and our in vivo imaging of MCC insertion provide an important foundation for future work, because mammalian MCCs—like the Xenopus MCCs studied here—arise from basally-positioned precursor cells (Evans and Moller, 1991; Rock et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Evans and Moller, 1991; Rock et al., 2010).
